ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Neurology (headache medicine) Consultation — Thomas Jefferson

code.originalText: Two-week review of the headache diary, seen the same day by headache medicine: diagnosis, acute treatment and the decision on preventive treatment

text.paragraph: Recurrent disabling headaches since his twenties, in bouts of near-daily morning-onset attacks lasting weeks, in a 47-year-old cabinet secretary now in the seventh day of a bout. Please confirm the diagnosis and advise on acute and preventive treatment. [S]
Urgency: Within two weeks, on the day of his two-week primary care review, with the headache diary. [S]

list.item: Do his headaches meet ICHD-3 criteria for migraine, and is any other primary or secondary headache likely?
Is neuroimaging or any other test needed?
What acute treatment do you advise, and what should he avoid?
Is preventive treatment indicated, and which medicine fits a man whose work depends on reading and writing?
How should we prevent medication overuse headache and manage long bouts?

text.paragraph: Mr. Jefferson, a 47-year-old cabinet secretary, is seen at the request of Dr. Beaumont-Ruiz with a 14-day headache diary. He has had headaches since about 20, coming in bouts that last from days to several weeks, every few years, often at times of heavy work. The present bout began three weeks ago. In the diary, headache came on 7 of 14 days, starting between nine and ten in the morning and lasting six to ten hours, throbbing and moderate to severe across the forehead and temples, worse with reading and climbing stairs, with light and noise sensitivity on every headache day and nausea on four. He has never had an aura. The last seven days have been free. Naproxen on four days helped partly. He stopped the combination analgesic at intake. He sleeps about six hours, drinks two cups of coffee a day and skips meals on busy days. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Thomas Jefferson was born at Shadwell, in what was then Goochland County, Virginia, on April 13, 1743 (April 2, 1743, in the Old Style calendar then in use). [D]
At 20, in a letter of March 20, 1764, written at Williamsburg late at night, he wrote of "a violent head ach, with which I have been afflicted these two days." [D]
In 1776 an illness kept him at home in Virginia for about six weeks longer than he intended; a correspondent wrote that his time at home had been interrupted by "an inveterate head ach." [D]

His wife died on September 6, 1782, of complications after childbirth. In November 1782 he wrote that he was only "a little emerging from that stupor of mind which had rendered me as dead to the world as she was whose loss occasioned it." [D]

In March 1784, at Annapolis as a delegate to Congress, he wrote that he had "lately added an attack of my periodical headach" to his habitual ill health and had to avoid reading, writing and almost thinking; his letters thereafter call the attacks his "periodical head-ach." [D]

In September 1786, in Paris, he dislocated his right wrist in a fall; the bones were set, but not well. He wrote with his left hand for a time, and in December 1788 wrote that the joint "had never been replaced," that he had lost the use of the hand "except that I can write," and that "a withered hand and swelled and crooked fingers" remained. [D]
After five years in France as a diplomat, he took office as the first Secretary of State in New York City on March 21, 1790. [D]
In New York, a periodical headache "came on me the 1st. of May" 1790, and the first week was violent; his account books record purchases of Peruvian bark (cinchona) on May 1 and May 3. [D]

text.paragraph: 12 later historical claims are omitted because they describe events after the index age. See the teaching note.

list.item: Migraine without aura, episodic, with bouts of near-daily attacks (G43.009). ICHD-3 criteria are met: at least five attacks of 4 to 72 hours with throbbing, moderate to severe pain worsened by routine activity, nausea, and light and noise sensitivity, not better accounted for by another diagnosis. Tension-type headache does not cause this severity, nausea or disability, though neck tension may add to it. Cluster headache does not fit: his attacks last hours, come by day, and lack one-sided eye symptoms. Medication overuse headache is not present, since the combination analgesic was used on fewer than 10 days a month and has stopped. [S]

Need for investigation (G43.009). A long, stable pattern with a normal neurological examination and no red flags does not call for brain imaging or blood tests; imaging would be considered for a new or changed pattern, a sudden severe headache, neurological signs, fever or onset after 50. [S]

Acute treatment (G43.009). Naproxen alone gives partial relief. A triptan with an NSAID taken early in the attack is the most effective first choice; he has no cardiovascular contraindication. A gepant or lasmiditan is the alternative if a triptan fails or becomes unsuitable. Opioids and butalbital should be avoided: they work poorly for migraine and raise the risk of medication overuse headache. [S]

Preventive treatment (G43.009). Bouts bring 13 migraine days in four weeks with severe disability (MIDAS 39), which meets the 2021 American Headache Society criteria for offering prevention. Propranolol is well established and inexpensive, and suits his normal blood pressure and lack of asthma. Topiramate can slow word-finding and concentration, and amitriptyline can cause morning drowsiness, both poor fits for his work. The 2024 AHS position statement makes a CGRP monoclonal antibody a first-line option, while the 2025 ACP guideline places it after the first-line oral preventives; after discussing both, he chose propranolol first, with an antibody as the next step. [S]
Old right wrist injury (M25.631). Neck and shoulder tension from long writing with a painful wrist may add to his headaches; hand therapy, a splint and dictation are worth doing. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Beaumont-Ruiz's intake note and the 14-day diary. MIDAS 39 (grade IV) and HIT-6 66 at intake; PHQ-9 6, GAD-7 7, AUDIT-C 3. Blood pressure 122/78 and pulse 70 today. No laboratory tests or imaging have been done, and none are needed. [S]

list.item: Sumatriptan 100 mg with naproxen 500 mg early in an attack, with a second sumatriptan after two hours if needed; no more than nine triptan days a month. [S]

Propranolol extended-release 80 mg each evening, raised to 120 mg at four weeks if pulse and blood pressure allow; judge the effect at two to three months, seeking at least half as many migraine days. [S]
A CGRP monoclonal antibody if propranolol is not tolerated or does not work. [S]
Keep acute medicine to two days a week or fewer, count the days in the diary, and avoid opioids, butalbital and combination products with caffeine. [S]
No brain imaging unless the pattern changes or red flags appear. [S]

For an attack lasting more than 72 hours, or a bout of daily attacks that the plan does not control, call the clinic for a short scheduled bridge (naproxen twice daily for up to five days) or treatment in clinic, rather than daily triptans or extra analgesics. [S]
A fixed wake time, regular meals, steady caffeine, daily walks, regular breaks from reading, and hand therapy and dictation for the wrist. [S]
PHQ-9 four to six weeks after starting propranolol, since beta-blockers can affect mood in some people. [S]

Discussed with Dr. Beaumont-Ruiz, who saw him the same day. The diagnosis and plan were explained to Mr. Jefferson, who asked careful questions about how each medicine works and chose propranolol after weighing the options. [S]
Follow-up: Dr. Beaumont-Ruiz continues care at four weeks and three months; headache medicine will see him again if prevention fails, the pattern changes, or an antibody is needed. [S]
